entities.name: Gigs
entities.how_described: 本集主线公司：像电信领域的 Stripe，让任何公司都能把手机套餐嵌入自家产品，从儿童智能手表做到 Revolut、Klarna、Cash App，累计融资 9000 万美元。

evidence.quote: Excited to have you here, man. So you've got a company called Gigs, which is like the OS for embedded telecoms. So, I mean, the simple way to think about it is anybody building anything can add Gigs into their product and offer, you know, mobile plans to their customers. So we're going to talk a lot about not just how you came up with that, but who is using that, who's the best customer, why they would want to do that and all those sort of things. You know, you raised your first round, I think, in 2021. You've raised $90 million since then. So off to a great start. Let's start with what we always do. For you, what was the product market fit moment? When did you feel like you'd found true product market fit and why?
evidence.speaker: Pablo Srugo

evidence.quote: So we had several product market fit moments. The very first was our first vertical. It was kids' smartwatches at the time. Very serendipitous. Indipitous first customer came through one of our advisors. And it was a great way to, like, find this niche to serve first. They had massive problems with SIM cards, returns of the devices, and monetizing the subscriptions. So we've built a product quite custom to that specific customer vertical. But it allowed us to build the very first version of Gigs and the API and integrations into carriers and paid for our seed in Series A. And we kept just going down the list of customers. And about a year in, we ended up powering most of the players in the market. And it kind of showed us, okay, like, there's definitely something there. And we found a repeatable motion. And then the next time was when we started targeting fintechs, which was our first real, like, consumer primary use case smartphone vertical. And NewBank was the very first customer in the fintech vertical. And then we kept repeating that again and again. We had Klarna and Revolut and so on. And it's, okay, we're winning over 90% of deals. Currently, we have product market fit. Once the services started launching in the last year and earlier this year, revenue skyrocketed. So we kind of understood, okay, we made it again. And now we're going through it the third time with Gigsawork, our enterprise product that we're targeting at enterprises that operate either in one or multiple markets, have a few hundred employees or more. And we allow them to embed the phone plan directly into their IT stack. So when an employee is provisioned on the HRS system and their Slack, Okta, and Gmail's provision, the phone number is provisioned in the same way in real time. And then also disconnected when the employee leaves. And we're in an inasancy of that product, but we're now also seeing a repeatable motion. So we're kind of carefully in the early stages of product market fit a third time. And we have a couple more verticals out of us.
evidence.speaker: Hermann Frank

evidence.quote: So it was my co-founder, Dennis and I, and Dennis and I are now co-founders on Gigs. And we had one intern, like a friend that was like helping us.

evidence.quote: Not paid, just users. That's how we came to Gigs when we tried to figure out the paid part.

evidence.quote: Yeah, sorry. I mean, at that point, right? So not the original idea, but like the first version of what GIGS is today.
evidence.speaker: Pablo Srugo

entities.name: Stripe
entities.how_described: 本集把它说成 Gigs 的叙事模板（『做手机套餐的 Stripe』），并提到不少早期 Stripe 员工因此加入 Gigs。

evidence.quote: Exactly. So we got gigabits upon gigabits of like free backhaul capacity out of it. And then about a year in, we're like, hey, this is clearly working. Like what are we going to do with it? Like we had plans to scale this to like 10 other markets. And we like tried to figure out how to monetize the best. And the idea was we're only in two neighborhoods. We don't have a desire to like cover the entire city. Like that's where... Like tourists are mostly here. And what we wanted to achieve is that you could buy an eSIM. And when you're within reach of our network, you would roam on our network and we would not pay anything for the traffic. But when you're not, you could roam on the national LTE network. And we were very much expecting to find an API to allow us to provision a device on the network and then tie in ourselves. So basically like a Stripe-like experience and telecoms, if you will. And it didn't exist. And we were very surprised as to why that doesn't exist. So like that kind of let us down a rabbit hole. And we understood that the industry just like was not able to produce this like developer experience, like this horizontal developer experience that we've kind of came to be used in pretty much every other industry, like hosting, payments, right? Like you just have an API for pretty much everything. And once we understood why and like what would happen if we would solve it, we understood, okay, this is the biggest problem we've ever seen.
evidence.speaker: Hermann Frank

evidence.quote: So the Stripe for telco was kind of the original idea.
evidence.speaker: Pablo Srugo

evidence.quote: Well, the Stripe for telco was what we discovered while building hardware and building Wi-Fi networks.
evidence.speaker: Hermann Frank

evidence.quote: so we were lucky in the beginning we had Stripe like Stripe was our projection we're building Stripe for phone plans that was the tagline that was the story and that resonated really well and quite early on we had quite a few people from Stripe call on board as team members they were early at Stripe and they saw the same thing this reminds me a lot of Stripe in its early days and they understood what this should be and what this could be the more we progressed the more this became kind of a real story arc and it's like only relatively recently where we said okay we kind of understand the market more now and there is more depth that we can go into where like that started kind of we can now start telling our own story and our own vision of the world but for the longest period we just used another highly successful company that we truly believe is a parallel to what we're building as an example and that allow people that don't understand much about telecom to understand okay yeah if they can make this work the mechanics work a similar way it's a similarly complex industry then they will be able to build a massive company so just use an existing example
evidence.speaker: Hermann Frank

evidence.quote: I'd say one of the other things that has worked really well for us is hire people who came up with the people working at your target customers we hire a lot of X-stripes the stripe mafia is everywhere they work in pretty much every company want their decision makers there so if you have someone who can go to 30 50 percent of your target list and they are well known and respected and trusted everybody is going to take a call everybody is going to listen and if you're in a competitive process you might have an advantage and trust as well this multi threading multi altitude in combination with having people who came up with the people that you want to work with is why we win as many deals as we do and you the listener will have but if you have a great product and do these things worked really well for us
evidence.speaker: Hermann Frank

evidence.quote: This is what I always find especially challenging when an idea depends on you bringing large enterprises into play as a tiny, you know, little startup with no credibility, no name, you know, relatively no funding. evidence.speaker: Pablo Srugo

evidence.quote: And so when we started telling people that that's what we want to do, like, and we started talking to first investors, we got no's left and right because they didn't talk to their buddy at like AT&T or to telecom and other funds. It's like, yeah, no carrier will ever let them do this, right? Like this is, this is not possible. People have tried and yada, yada. So we kind of had to chew our way through it. Like the way we actually got our first deal done was not even with a carrier because they wouldn't talk to us. So that part was actually true initially. We found an aggregator that was behind on their commitments with the network and we integrated there and we built the first version of the product on that aggregator with terrible economics, right? We didn't make any money on that.
evidence.speaker: Hermann Frank

evidence.quote: Exactly. We were just able to plug into the same integration that they had and for the first use case we had, it worked fine. Like, it would never work for like what we're doing today but like it worked fine for that kids' smartwatch use case. And then we started onboarding customers there and we went to the network and said like, hey, we build a product like on your network and like here's what it does and here's like where we are. evidence.speaker: Hermann Frank

And then at some point when people are actually staying with your product and they're not turned off by it after a couple of weeks or months and you've been able to build a scalable sales motion, then you actually might have it.
